El método de la escuela: probar divisore: The school method: trying divisors from 2 upwards. Reaching $\sqrt{n}$ is enough, because a composite always has a factor below it. For an $n$ of $b$ bits that is $2^{b/2}$ divisions: with 2048 bits, $2^{1024}$, a 309-digit number of divisions. The age of the universe in nanoseconds has 27. En 1975 John Pollard tuvo una idea que p: In 1975 John Pollard had an idea that seems to have nothing to do with it: iterate a random function modulo $n$, for instance $x \mapsto x^2 + 1$, and wait for two values to coincide modulo $p$, the unknown factor. You do not need to know $p$ to detect it: if $x_i \equiv x_j \pmod p$, then $p$ divides $x_i - x_j$, and $\gcd(x_i - x_j, n)$ hands it over. By the birthday paradox, the coincidence modulo $p$ arrives after about $\sqrt{p}$ steps, and since $p \le \sqrt n$, that is $n^{1/4}$ steps.
Estos algoritmos son los que fijan el ta: These algorithms are what set everybody's key sizes: when RSA-768 fell in 2009, 1024-bit keys came to be considered insufficient, and browsers stopped accepting them. Pollard rho also has a life of its own outside factoring: the same tortoise and hare finds collisions in hash functions and discrete logarithms on elliptic curves, and it is the best known attack against them. And the sieves were the first great distributed computation over the internet, with volunteers from all over the world.
Factorizar un número de 617 cifras no es: Factoring a 617-digit number is not impossible in principle: you can go on trying divisors, and at some point it ends. The problem is the time. What separates a secure system from a broken one is the cost curve: how the time to factor grows with the size of the number. Ingenious methods move that curve, and every time they have moved it, keys have had to grow.
Fermat describió su método en una carta: Fermat described his method in a letter of 1643. John Pollard published rho in 1975, and in 1974 another method, $p - 1$, which finds factors $p$ such that $p - 1$ has only small factors; RSA keys are generated so as to avoid it. Carl Pomerance invented the quadratic sieve in 1981, and Pollard proposed in 1988 the number field sieve, which Arjen Lenstra, Hendrik Lenstra and others developed. Martin Gardner's RSA-129 challenge of 1977, which its authors estimated would be secure for forty trillion years, was solved in seventeen.
